lessons.prologue: In AD 762, one hundred thousand builders raised a dazzling circular capital beside the River Tigris! Step through Baghdad’s four great gates, explore the Green Dome Palace at the City of Peace, and discover why this Silk Road crossroads dwarfed Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain.
lessons.blurb: In AD 762, one hundred thousand builders raised a dazzling circular capital beside the River Tigris! Step through Baghdad’s four great gates, explore the Green Dome Palace at the City of Peace, and discover why this Silk Road crossroads dwarfed Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain.

teacher_notes.primer: This opening Key Stage 2 enquiry introduces the rapid spread of early Islam from Arabia before focusing on Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur’s decision to found Baghdad in AD 762. Primary pupils investigate why the fertile bend between the Tigris and Euphrates was a Silk Road crossroads, how 100,000 bricklayers built the 2km circular Round City (Madinat al-Salam), and how Baghdad’s nearly one million citizens around AD 900 contrasted starkly with Anglo-Saxon Britain’s small timber towns of 5,000–10,000 people.

items.question: On a history timeline, did AD 762 happen before or after the Romans left Britain around AD 410?
items.answer: After the Romans left Britain (more than 350 years later)
items.explanation: AD dates count upwards from AD 1, so AD 762 came three and a half centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.

items.question: Why did so many ancient and medieval rulers choose to build capital cities beside major rivers?
items.answer: Rivers provided fresh drinking water, watered farm crops, and carried heavy trading boats
items.explanation: Before railways or lorries, river boats and canals were the fastest way to move food, bricks, and trade goods.

items.question: What was the famous network of overland trade routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, and the Mediterranean called?
items.answer: The Silk Roads (or Silk Road)
items.explanation: Caravans of camels and horses carried silk, spices, paper, glass, and ideas thousands of kilometres across Asia.

items.question: Which people ruled small kingdoms of wooden halls and farming villages across England around AD 900?
items.answer: The Anglo-Saxons (alongside Viking settlers in northern and eastern England)
items.explanation: Around AD 900, Anglo-Saxon Britain had small fortified *burh* towns of wooden houses rather than giant stone or brick cities.

items.question: What do historians mean when they call a group of many lands governed by one supreme ruler an "empire"?
items.answer: A large collection of countries, peoples, and cities united under a single ruler or government
items.explanation: In the early Islamic world, this vast empire was called a Caliphate and was led by a ruler known as a Caliph.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 610–762: Rapid Spread of Early Islam & Choosing the River Tigris
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Beginning in **Arabia**, the faith of **Islam** spread swiftly across wide lands. In **AD 750**, the **Abbasid** [uh-BASS-id] family took charge of this empire, led by a **Caliph**. In **AD 762**, **Caliph al-Mansur** [al-man-SOOR] searched for a safe central spot for his **capital**. He chose a fertile green bend on the **River Tigris**.

[1.2] Deep **canals** linked the Tigris straight to the **River Euphrates**. Fresh water fed lush date palms and golden wheat fields. Round woven-reed **quffa** [KOOF-uh] boats brought silk and spices, while Silk Road camel caravans met there.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 762–766: 100,000 Builders & the Round City of Peace
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Al-Mansur gathered **100,000 bricklayers** and diggers to raise the circular **Round City** of **Baghdad**. Architects first traced a circle **two kilometres** wide in flaming cotton seeds! Builders then baked millions of mud bricks for thick **double walls** and a deep moat. Al-Mansur named his capital **Madinat al-Salam** [mah-DEE-nat al-sah-LAHM], meaning **City of Peace**.

[1.4] Four guarded iron gates pierced the walls, named **Kufa**, **Basra**, **Khorasan**, and **Syria**. Straight market streets led towards the open centre. Right at the heart stood the **Great Mosque** beside the **Green Dome Palace**.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: One Million Citizens vs Anglo-Saxon Britain
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] Busy markets, bathhouses, and gardens soon spread beyond the Round City walls. By **AD 900**, bustling **Baghdad** was home to nearly **one million people**! Families strolled down **paved streets** beside cool **canals** and studied inside grand **libraries**.

[1.6] Meanwhile, towns in **Anglo-Saxon Britain** around **AD 900** looked tiny by comparison. Even major English towns like **London** or **Winchester** held only **5,000 to 10,000 people**. Most British families lived in smoky **timber huts** with thatched roofs. Muddy village lanes showed how huge Baghdad truly was!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain why Caliph al-Mansur chose the River Tigris in AD 762 and built Baghdad as a circle.
tasks.starter: In AD 762, Caliph al-Mansur chose a fertile bend on the River Tigris for his circular capital because...
hints: Explain how canals joined the Tigris and Euphrates rivers to water crops and welcome Silk Road boats.
Describe the two-kilometre double brick walls, four gates, and central Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace.
Explain what placing the palace and mosque in the exact centre of Madinat al-Salam symbolised to visitors!
tasks.model_answer: In AD 762, Caliph al-Mansur chose a fertile bend on the River Tigris for his circular capital because deep canals connected it straight to the River Euphrates, watering orchards and linking river boats with Silk Road camel caravans. Using 100,000 builders, he raised the two-kilometre double brick walls of Madinat al-Salam (the City of Peace) pierced by four gates pointing across the empire. Placing the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace at the exact centre showed that faith and the Caliph’s peaceful rule anchored the whole world!

lessons.prologue: Step inside Baghdad’s legendary House of Wisdom, where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators worked side by side! Discover how cheap rag paper from Samarkand filled over a hundred bookshops, while Fatima al-Fihri and Queen Zubayda funded learning and desert wells.

teacher_notes.primer: This second Key Stage 2 enquiry explores how Baghdad’s House of Wisdom (*Bayt al-Hikma*) under Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun united technological innovation with cultural exchange. narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 786–833: Harun al-Rashid, Al-Ma’mun & the Paper Revolution
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Under **Caliph Harun al-Rashid** and his son **Caliph al-Ma'mun** [al-mah-MOON], Baghdad drew thinkers from afar. Together they expanded a royal library into the **House of Wisdom**, or **Bayt al-Hikma** [bayt al-HIK-mah]. Via the Silk Road city of **Samarkand**, craftworkers learned Chinese **paper-making**. Watermills beat old cotton and linen rags into smooth, cheap paper.

[2.2] Across **Europe**, scribes still scraped costly **calfskin parchment** from whole cattle herds! Cheap rag paper transformed Baghdad's **book markets**. Soon over **100 bookshops** buzzed in the **Paper Sellers' Market** with poetry and star charts.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 830–900: The Translation Movement & Hunayn ibn Ishaq
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Al-Ma'mun sent messengers to buy rare ancient scrolls from Greece, Persia, and India. Inside the House of Wisdom, the **Translation Movement** rescued fragile books before they crumbled. **Muslim**, **Christian**, and **Jewish** scholars worked together turning **Greek**, **Persian**, and **Sanskrit** texts into **Arabic**.

[2.4] Their star translator was **Hunayn ibn Ishaq** [hoo-NAYN ib-in is-HAHK], a gifted Christian doctor. Stories say al-Ma'mun paid him the weight of every finished book in gold! Baghdad's scholars never copied old writers blindly. Instead, they tested every claim and fixed mistakes.

narrative_blocks.text:

tasks.question: Big Question: How did cheap paper and Baghdad’s House of Wisdom rescue and expand world knowledge?
tasks.starter: Rescuing and spreading Golden Age knowledge took an extraordinary team effort across the Islamic world...
hints: Explain how Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun funded the House of Wisdom and gathered rare scrolls.

tasks.model_answer: Rescuing and spreading Golden Age knowledge took an extraordinary team effort across the Islamic world. Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun provided royal funding to expand the House of Wisdom and send messengers for rare scrolls. Yet without skilled Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq, those Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books could never have been read, tested, and improved in Arabic on cheap rag paper. Equally important, visionary women patrons like Fatima al-Fihri — who founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in AD 859 — and Queen Zubayda kept students learning and travellers safe!

teacher_notes.primer: This third Key Stage 2 enquiry celebrates scientific, mathematical, engineering, and medical breakthroughs across the Islamic Golden Age (c. source_context.Source A: Working in Baghdad’s House of Wisdom, Muhammad al-Khwarizmi championed digits 0–9 (including zero, sifr) and wrote al-Jabr, giving us "algebra" and "algorithm". **Hinge Question:** Why is multiplying or dividing numbers like 408 by 12 so much easier with 0–9 and zero than with Roman numerals like CCCCVIII?
source_context.Source B: Skilled makers — including tenth-century woman astronomer Mariam al-Asturlabi in Aleppo — engraved rotating brass astrolabes that worked like pocket star computers. **Hinge Question:** How could holding a pocket-sized brass astrolabe up to the stars help both sea captains and worshippers on land?
source_context.Source C: Surgeon al-Zahrawi drew over 200 metal surgical tools so trainee doctors knew the exact shape and safe use of every instrument, alongside dissolving catgut stitches. **Hinge Question:** Why did al-Zahrawi draw clear pictures of all 200 surgical tools instead of only describing them in words?
source_context.Source D: Every major Islamic bimaristan (free hospital) ran its own inspected pharmacy where trained pharmacists measured syrups, balms, and herbal medicines. **Hinge Question:** Why was having a clean, inspected pharmacy right inside a free bimaristan hospital so helpful for sick patients?

items.question: Why did Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur build the Round City of Baghdad (Madinat al-Salam) on the River Tigris in AD 762?
items.answer: Canals linked the Tigris and Euphrates for fertile farming and boat trade right where Silk Road routes met
items.explanation: 100,000 workers raised a circular brick capital with four gates and the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace at its heart.

items.question: How did Baghdad around AD 900 contrast with towns in Anglo-Saxon Britain?
items.answer: Baghdad had nearly one million people with paved streets and libraries, while Anglo-Saxon towns held 5,000–10,000 in timber huts
items.explanation: Baghdad was the largest city in the western world at a time when British settlements were much smaller farming towns.

items.question: Through which Silk Road city did paper-making reach Baghdad, and how did rag paper beat European parchment?
items.answer: Via Samarkand; cotton-and-rag paper was smooth and cheap compared with costly scraped calfskin parchment
items.explanation: Affordable rag paper sparked over 100 bustling bookshops in Baghdad’s Paper Sellers’ Market.

items.question: Which faiths worked together in the House of Wisdom’s Translation Movement, led by medical translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq?
items.answer: Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars worked side by side translating Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books into Arabic
items.explanation: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was a Christian physician whose clear Arabic medical translations were prized by Caliph al-Ma’mun.

items.question: How did women patrons Fatima al-Fihri (AD 859) and Queen Zubayda leave lasting legacies?
items.answer: Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, and Queen Zubayda funded stone wells along the desert Hajj road to Mecca
items.explanation: Both women used their wealth to support education, travellers, and public welfare across the Islamic world.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 820–1206: Zero, Algebra, Astrolabes & the Elephant Clock
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] In **Baghdad's** House of Wisdom, **Muhammad al-Khwarizmi** [al-kwah-RIZ-mee] championed **Hindu-Arabic numerals** from **0 to 9**. Using **zero**, called **sifr** [SIF-er], made big sums far easier than clumsy Roman numerals! His **maths** book **al-Jabr** gave us **algebra**, and his own name gave us **algorithm**.

[3.2] Makers like **Mariam al-Asturlabi** [al-as-toor-LAH-bee] crafted brass **astrolabes** to map bright stars. Travellers held them up to check prayer times, sail seas, and find **Mecca**. Engineer **al-Jazari** [al-jah-ZAH-ree] also built **clocks** like his **Elephant Water Clock**. Hidden floats clashed brass cymbals every half hour to advance **science**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 965–1040: Ibn al-Haytham’s Light Proof & Free Bimaristans
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Ancient Greek writers once claimed invisible rays shot out of human eyes to see! Scientist **Ibn al-Haytham** [IB-in al-HAY-thum] doubted that story and tested **light** carefully. Inside a dark room with a tiny hole, he built a pinhole **camera obscura**. He proved light travels in **straight lines** into our eyes, inspiring modern cameras!

[3.4] Islamic cities also built free teaching hospitals called **bimaristans** [bee-MAH-rih-stahnz] for rich and poor alike. Each **bimaristan** had **clean wards**, cool fountains, and a stocked **pharmacy**. Recovering patients even got clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900–1013: Master Doctors Al-Razi & Al-Zahrawi
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] Before building Baghdad's hospital, chief doctor **al-Razi** [al-RAH-zee] hung fresh meat across town. He picked the spot where meat rotted slowest because the air was cleanest! Careful bedside notes helped al-Razi tell **measles** apart from **smallpox**. Trained nurses served healthy meals to help **sick people** recover.

[3.6] In Spain around **AD 1000**, royal surgeon **al-Zahrawi** [al-zah-RAH-wee] wrote an illustrated medical guide. He drew over **200 surgical tools**, including forceps, scalpels, and delicate bone saws. He also discovered **catgut stitches** that dissolved **safely** inside wounds as patients began to **heal**!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Ibn al-Haytham and doctor al-Razi used clever experiments instead of guesswork.
tasks.starter: Both Ibn al-Haytham and Baghdad doctor al-Razi proved the power of real scientific testing because...
hints: Describe how Ibn al-Haytham used a dark pinhole room (camera obscura) to prove light enters our eyes in straight lines.
Describe how al-Razi hung fresh meat around Baghdad to pick the cleanest-air hospital site.

tasks.model_answer: Both Ibn al-Haytham and Baghdad doctor al-Razi proved the power of real scientific testing because neither scholar accepted old claims without evidence. When ancient Greek books claimed rays shot out of human eyes, Ibn al-Haytham built a pitch-dark pinhole camera obscura and proved light actually travels in straight lines into our eyes! Similarly, al-Razi hung fresh meat across Baghdad to build his bimaristan where meat rotted slowest in clean air, and kept detailed bedside notes to distinguish measles from smallpox.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Golden Age mathematicians, astronomers, engineers, and doctors change world science forever?
tasks.starter: Although maths, optics, and medicine all transformed human life, I think the biggest Golden Age breakthrough was...
hints: Compare al-Khwarizmi’s 0–9 numerals, zero (sifr), algebra, and algorithms with Mariam al-Asturlabi’s astrolabes.
Weigh up Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura light proof and free bimaristan hospitals.
Reach a clear judgement explaining how your chosen breakthrough connects to the other two in modern life!
tasks.model_answer: Although maths, optics, and medicine all transformed human life, I think al-Khwarizmi’s mathematics changed our modern world the most because every other science depends on it! His Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9 including zero, sifr), algebra, and step-by-step algorithms power modern computers, engineering, and hospital machines alike. Even so, Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura gave us eyeglasses and cameras, while free bimaristans, al-Razi’s clinical notes, and al-Zahrawi’s 200 surgical tools and dissolving catgut stitches created the blueprint for modern healthcare!

teacher_notes.primer: This fourth Key Stage 2 enquiry explores Baghdad's global trade networks between c. AD 850 and 1000. Primary pupils trace overland Silk Road camel caravans stopping every 30 km at fortified caravanserais, maritime dhow voyages from Basra across the Indian Ocean using astrolabes, and early paper cheques (sakk). Crucially, pupils connect Baghdad directly to British history through Abbasid silver dirham hoards found around Viking Jorvik (York) and Anglo-Saxon King Offa of Mercia's gold imitation dinar.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 850–1000: Covered Bazaars, Silk Caravans & Roadside Caravanserais
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] **Baghdad** sat where Asia, Africa, and Europe met, making its **markets** world famous. Shaded **bazaars**, or **souks**, smelled of Indian pepper, cardamom, and sweet cinnamon. Stalls gleamed with Chinese silk, white porcelain, Persian rugs, and blown glass. Long **caravans** of two-humped **camels** crossed hot **Silk Road** desert **trails**.

[4.2] Every **thirty kilometres** along the road stood a **walled** **inn** called a **caravanserai** [kar-uh-VAN-suh-ry]. Locked brick gates kept traders safe from desert bandits at night. Tired camels drank cool well water while merchants shared spiced stews by firelight!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 850–1000: Indian Ocean Dhow Ships & Paper Sakk Cheques
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] River boats also carried crates south down the Tigris to the busy sea port of **Basra**. Sailors loaded wooden **dhow** [DOW] ships built from planks stitched tightly with coconut rope! Tall triangular sails caught ocean winds across the **Indian Ocean** towards India and China. Captains steered safely at night by checking star heights with brass **astrolabes**.

[4.4] Carrying heavy coin sacks on **long-distance trade** risked bandit or pirate attacks. Clever Baghdad bankers solved this by writing signed paper slips called a **sakk** [SAHK]. Merchants cashed them safely afar, giving English our word **cheque**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 774–1000: Viking Silver Dirhams in Jorvik & King Offa’s Gold Coin
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Silver **trade coins** struck for **Baghdad's** caliphs even reached snowy **Scandinavia** and **Britain**! Pure Abbasid silver **dirhams** [DEER-hamz] with Arabic script flowed north up Russian rivers. **Vikings** prized this trusted silver for buying furs and swords. tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how caravanserais and paper sakk cheques helped Silk Road merchants travel safely.
tasks.starter: Crossing thousands of miles of desert and sea was dangerous for medieval traders, so...
hints: Explain how walled brick caravanserais stood every thirty kilometres with courtyard wells and strong gates.

tasks.model_answer: Crossing thousands of miles of desert and sea was dangerous for medieval traders, so rulers built walled brick caravanserais every thirty kilometres along the Silk Road. Behind locked gates, camel caravans rested safely from desert bandits, drank fresh well water, and shared news. In addition, Baghdad bankers invented signed paper payment slips called a sakk — giving us our English word cheque — so merchants could travel without carrying heavy sacks of gold coins!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did land caravans and sea dhows make Baghdad a trading superpower, and how did Islamic coins reach Britain?
tasks.starter: Between AD 850 and 1000, Baghdad's traders linked three continents, and astonishing coin clues even connect them to Britain...
hints: Describe Baghdad’s east-west reach first — Silk Road camel caravans to China and Basra dhows across the Indian Ocean.

Finish with Anglo-Saxon King Offa of Mercia minting an AD 774 gold coin copying an Abbasid Arabic dinar!
tasks.model_answer: Between AD 850 and 1000, Baghdad's traders linked three continents, and astonishing coin clues even connect them to Britain. Eastwards, camel caravans trekked the Silk Road to China while wooden dhow ships sailed from Basra across the Indian Ocean for pepper, cardamom, and pearls. Northwards, pure Abbasid silver dirhams flowed along Russian rivers to Viking traders, who buried thousands of them in hoards across Scandinavia and near Jorvik (York). Even Anglo-Saxon King Offa of Mercia minted a gold coin around AD 774 copying an Arabic dinar!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: Cool Courtyard Houses, Windcatchers & Public Hammams
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Summer afternoons in Iraq blazed hot, yet **Baghdad's** builders kept **homes** wonderfully **cool**. Thick brick walls sheltered shaded inner **courtyards** splashed by stone fountains and orange trees. Above the roofs rose tall **windcatcher** towers, called **badgirs** [bad-GEERZ], facing the breeze. They scooped cool outdoor air down indoors while pushing hot air out!

[5.2] Keeping **clean** mattered deeply before daily prayers and **families'** meals. Every district had steamed public bathhouses called **hammams** [hah-MAHMZ] with tiled hot and cool rooms. Bathers scrubbed with olive-oil **soap** bars and splashed sweet **rosewater**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: Citrus Orchards, Spiced Kitchens & Geometric Mosque Art
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Around **AD 900**, canal waterwheels fed lush orchards around **Baghdad** filled with tasty new **foods**. Farmers grew tangy **lemons**, sweet **oranges**, purple **aubergines**, green **spinach**, and ruby **pomegranates**. Cooks simmered spiced stews with crushed **almonds** and **cane sugar**. Families served warm dishes on shiny metallic **lustreware** bowls.

[5.4] Inside mosques, **art styles** avoided human or animal statues so worshippers honoured God alone. Using compasses, tilers made eight-pointed **geometric** stars and curling **arabesque** [ar-uh-BESK] leaf vines. Sacred **Arabic calligraphy** from the Qur'an completed every wall in calm symmetry!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: Silk Tiraz Robes, Glass Mosque Lamps & Shatranj Chess
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] Skilled workshops helped **people** in **Baghdad** **dress** finely and **light** their **homes**. Royal looms wove bright silk robes trimmed with embroidered Arabic name bands called **tiraz** [tee-RAHZ]. Master glassblowers also gilded enamelled glass **mosque lamps** inscribed with glowing verses.

[5.6] When evening breezes cooled the courtyard, families sat on woven carpets. Guests sipped sweet fruit syrups with rosewater and loved to **play** strategy games! Everyone prized **shatranj** [shat-RANJ], the ancient board game that became **chess**. Clever winners cried *Shah mat*, giving English our word **checkmate**!

narrative_blocks.title: January–February AD 1258: Hulagu Khan & the Mongol Siege of Baghdad
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Over centuries, the huge Abbasid Empire split into smaller rival kingdoms. **Baghdad** stayed proud in learning, yet its weak army could not guard wide borders. In **January 1258**, a vast **Mongol army** led by **Hulagu Khan** [hoo-LAH-goo KAHN] marched from Central Asia. Thousands of horsemen surrounded Baghdad along both banks of the River Tigris.

[6.2] Mongol engineers built giant wooden **trebuchets** [TREB-yoo-shets] that hurled heavy boulders at Baghdad's brick walls. In **February 1258**, Mongol troops stormed through the broken walls. Fires ruined palaces, canals, and the **House of Wisdom**, ending Abbasid rule.

narrative_blocks.title: Cairo, Córdoba & Toledo: Why Golden Age Knowledge Survived
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] Did **Golden Age** **knowledge** vanish in **1258** when Baghdad's library burned? Thankfully not, because paper copies sat safely in **cities** like **Cairo**, **Damascus**, and **Samarkand**! Far west in Islamic Spain, called **Al-Andalus** [al-AN-duh-loos], **Córdoba** [KOR-doh-bah] shone with street lamps and seventy libraries. Rulers there also built Granada's carved **Alhambra** palace.

[6.4] Next, Spanish **Toledo** became Europe's bridge for rescuing Arabic science. Muslim, Jewish, and Christian translators worked side by side there. Turning **al-Khwarizmi**, **Ibn al-Haytham**, and **Ibn Sina** [IB-in SEE-nah] into **Latin** helped spark Europe's **Renaissance**!

narrative_blocks.title: From 1258 to Today: Arabic Words & Ideas in Our Everyday Lives
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] **Today**, the **Early Islamic** **Golden Age** still shapes **our lives** at school and home! Writing digits **0 to 9**, solving **algebra**, or running a phone **algorithm** uses Baghdad's maths. **Ibn al-Haytham's** light tests led straight to glasses, microscopes, and smartphone cameras. Clean hospital wards and pharmacies also build on Islamic medicine.

[6.6] You even speak everyday Arabic words like **zero**, **chemistry**, **sugar**, **lemon**, and **orange**! Cosy home words like **sofa** and **cotton** arrived through Arabic trade too. Though Baghdad's walls fell in **1258**, Golden Age ideas live on!

tasks.model_answer: Although Hulagu Khan destroyed Baghdad’s House of Wisdom in February 1258, the Golden Age never truly disappeared because books and ideas proved tougher than brick walls! Copies already thrived in Cairo, Damascus, Samarkand, Córdoba, and the Alhambra, while Toledo’s translators shared them in Latin to spark Europe’s Renaissance. Today, every time we write 0–9, solve algebra, run a phone algorithm, focus a camera lens, or say zero, chemistry, sugar, lemon, orange, sofa, and cotton, Baghdad’s Golden Age lives on!

key_individuals.name: Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (AD 714–775)
key_individuals.role: Second Abbasid Caliph & Visionary Founder of the Round City of Baghdad
key_individuals.origins: Born into the Abbasid family descended from the Prophet Muhammad’s uncle al-Abbas; searched Iraq personally in AD 762 for a breezy, fertile riverside crossroads.
key_individuals.significance: Chose a strategic bend on the River Tigris linked by canals to the Euphrates and laid out Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace") as a geometric circle two kilometres wide.
achievements: Gathered around 100,000 builders, bricklayers, and surveyors in AD 762 to raise Baghdad’s double brick walls, deep moat, and four great gates.
Placed the Green Dome Palace and Great Mosque right at the heart of the Round City, facing roads towards Basra, Kufa, Khorasan, and Damascus.
Started the royal palace library collection of Persian, Greek, and Sanskrit books that blossomed into Baghdad’s famous House of Wisdom.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Traced Baghdad’s giant circular street plan onto the ground with lines of cotton seeds soaked in oil and lit them with fire so he could inspect the layout from above!

key_individuals.name: Caliph Harun al-Rashid & Queen Zubayda (c. AD 766–831)
key_individuals.role: Fifth Abbasid Caliph & Royal Patroness of Scholars, Hospitals & Desert Water Engineering
key_individuals.origins: Royal cousins who presided over Baghdad at the height of its wealth and fame, remembered in history books and The Thousand and One Nights alike.
key_individuals.significance: Turned Baghdad into a magnet for global translators, doctors, poets, and diplomats while funding major public works that served ordinary travellers.
achievements: Harun al-Rashid expanded the royal House of Wisdom, founded Baghdad’s first free bimaristan hospital, and sent diplomatic gifts — including an Asian elephant and brass water clock — to Emperor Charlemagne!
Queen Zubayda funded the 1,400-kilometre Darb Zubayda desert road from Iraq to Mecca, paying engineers to blast rock cisterns, wells, and milestones for thirsty pilgrims.
Patronised paper mills, silk tiraz workshops, and pure gold dinar and silver dirham mints trusted from China to northern Europe.
key_individuals.key_distinction: When engineers warned Queen Zubayda that carving desert wells would cost a fortune, she famously replied to build it even if every single pickaxe blow cost a coin of pure gold!

key_individuals.name: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. AD 780–850)
key_individuals.role: House of Wisdom Mathematician, Astronomer & "Father of Algebra"
key_individuals.origins: Born around Khwarazm near the Aral Sea in Central Asia before moving to Baghdad under Caliph al-Ma’mun to lead maths and astronomy research in the House of Wisdom.
key_individuals.significance: Revolutionised world mathematics by championing place-value Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9, including sifr / zero) and inventing step-by-step equation-solving.
achievements: Wrote Kitab al-Jabr around AD 820 to help people calculate inheritances, land measurements, and canal digging — giving every language the word "algebra"!
Explained how zero (sifr) works as a place-holder so merchants and scientists could add, subtract, and multiply far faster than with Roman numerals.
Calculated accurate star tables and revised world maps with seventy fellow geographers; the Latin spelling of his name (Algoritmi) gave us "algorithm"!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Every single search engine, video game, and smartphone app running on "algorithms" today carries the name of this 9th-century Baghdad mathematician!

key_individuals.name: Fatima al-Fihri & Mariam al-Asturlabi (9th–10th Century AD)
key_individuals.role: Pioneering Female Patron of Learning & Master Maker of Brass Astrolabes
key_individuals.origins: Fatima al-Fihri grew up in an educated merchant family moving from Kairouan to Fez in Morocco; a century later, Mariam al-Asturlabi trained in precision brass engineering in Syria.
key_individuals.significance: Prove that women played vital roles in early Islamic scholarship and scientific instrument-making, funding seats of higher learning and crafting complex sky computers.
achievements: In AD 859, Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found al-Qarawiyyin in Fez — still operating in Morocco over 1,160 years later as the world’s oldest continually running degree-granting institution!
Mariam al-Asturlabi hand-engraved intricate brass planispheric astrolabes so accurate that the ruler of Aleppo hired her at his royal court.
Enabled sailors on Indian Ocean dhows, desert travellers, and astronomers to tell time by the stars and find the exact direction of Mecca.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Modern astronomers named main-belt asteroid 7060 Al-Ijliya in honour of Mariam al-Asturlabi’s dazzling brass star-mapping instruments!

key_individuals.name: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, c. AD 965–1040)
key_individuals.role: Physicist, Astronomer, Pioneer of Optics & Champion of the Scientific Method
key_individuals.origins: Born in the Iraqi port city of Basra during the Islamic Golden Age and later worked beside Cairo’s great libraries and mosques.
key_individuals.significance: Overturned ancient Greek guesses that invisible beams shot out of human eyes, using dark-room experiments to prove light travels in straight lines into our eyes.
achievements: Built a darkened pinhole chamber (al-bayt al-muzlim — Latin camera obscura) showing how light rays pass through a tiny hole to project an upside-down image.
Wrote the seven-volume Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir), explaining reflection, refraction, rainbows, lenses, and how the eye’s cornea and optic nerve work.
Insisted scientists must doubt untested claims and check every idea with repeatable experiments — a cornerstone of the modern scientific method!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Known in Latin Europe as "Alhazen", his pinhole dark-room experiments paved the way for reading glasses, telescopes, microscopes, and every camera on Earth!

key_individuals.name: Al-Razi & Al-Zahrawi (9th–10th Century AD)
key_individuals.role: Chief Baghdad Hospital Physician & Pioneering Surgeon of Al-Andalus
key_individuals.origins: Al-Razi (Rhazes) directed major bimaristan hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, while al-Zahrawi (Albucasis) practised surgery near Córdoba in Islamic Spain.
key_individuals.significance: Transformed medieval medicine from superstition into careful clinical observation, hygienic hospital care, and illustrated surgical training.
achievements: Before choosing where to build Baghdad’s new hospital, al-Razi hung fresh meat around the city and picked the spot where it rotted slowest — proving the air there was cleanest!
Al-Razi wrote the first clear medical guide telling measles apart from smallpox and compiled gigantic medical encyclopaedias used for centuries.

Al-Zahrawi wrote a thirty-volume medical guide illustrating over 200 surgical instruments — forceps, scalpels, bone saws — and pioneered internal stitches made from natural catgut that dissolved harmlessly as patients healed!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Translated into Latin in Spain, al-Razi’s and al-Zahrawi’s illustrated books trained European doctors and surgeons for more than five hundred years!

guided_reading.extract: Warm breezes rippled across the River Tigris in summer AD 762 as Caliph al-Mansur stood on a green plain. Round woven quffa boats bobbed along deep canals linking the Tigris and Euphrates. "Here is the finest crossroads on Earth!" the Caliph smiled. Ships from China and India could meet Silk Road camel trains right at his gates. Instead of tangled lanes, al-Mansur planned a giant round city two kilometres wide. Builders pegged cords into the soil and poured white ash lines for double brick walls and four gates. Still, how could the Caliph see the whole huge circle at once? At dusk, workers laid trails of fluffy cottonseeds soaked in lamp oil along every ash line. Torches touched the trail—whoosh! Two bright rings of golden fire blazed out across the dark plain! Standing right in the middle, proud al-Mansur ordered 100,000 builders to raise Madinat al-Salam, his City of Peace.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Caliph al-Mansur ask his workmen to lay oil-soaked cottonseeds along the ash lines at night?

parent_discussion.question: How would a traveller arriving from a muddy Anglo-Saxon timber village around AD 900 have felt entering million-strong Baghdad?

guided_reading.author_context: Born in Baghdad, 9th-century traveller Ahmad al-Ya'qubi walked through his home city's markets taking vivid notes. Listen to his eyewitness wonder at a city buzzing with cheap rag paper and over a hundred bookshops!

guided_reading.extract: Around AD 891, Baghdad writer Ahmad al-Ya'qubi walked past splashing watermills and shaded arches to describe his home city. "I start my book with Baghdad because it stands at the heart of the world! No other city from East to West can match it. Cool river breezes blow in summer, and green gardens ring every street. Wooden boats glide up the Tigris bringing silks and spices from India, China, and Africa." "Walk down the Street of the Booksellers, and you will count over one hundred busy bookshops side by side! Watermills beat old linen and cotton rags into smooth white paper far cheaper than animal skin. Inside the shops, scribes copy poems and star maps. guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in Muhammad al-Khwarizmi's math treatises (c. AD 820), al-Razi's Baghdad hospital records (c. AD 900), and Ismail al-Jazari's illustrated 'Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices' (AD 1206).
guided_reading.author_context: Try multiplying Roman numerals like MMDCCXLVIII in your head—no wonder sums took hours! Discover how scholars in the Islamic world gave us 0–9 numbers, free hospitals, and a robot elephant clock!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Illuminated Arabic manuscript page from engineer al-Jazari's AD 1206 book showing his colourful mechanical Elephant Water Clock.

vocabVault.def: Baghdad's star mathematician whose books gave us 0–9 place-value numbers, 'algebra' (al-Jabr), and 'algorithm'.
The Arabic word for empty or 'zero'—the clever placeholder digit that makes large sums quick and accurate.
A clean, free Islamic teaching hospital with separate wards, fountains, pharmacies, and trained nurses.
The brilliant 12th–13th century Islamic engineer who designed automatic water clocks and mechanical machines.

guided_reading.extract: In Baghdad's House of Wisdom around AD 820, scholar al-Khwarizmi wrote ten neat signs on white paper. He used digits `1` to `9` plus a small circle called sifr—our word zero! With zero holding empty places, traders solved big sums fast while Europe used slow Roman letters. Better still, his book al-Jabr gave us algebra, and his name gave us algorithm! Across town, doctor al-Razi welcomed rich nobles and poor guests alike into Baghdad's free bimaristan hospital. Cool fountains splashed in clean wards while nurses served fresh food. Leaving patients even got clean clothes and coins so they could rest at home! Later in AD 1206, builder al-Jazari unveiled his tall Elephant Water Clock. Inside the brass elephant floated a copper bowl with a tiny hole. Every half hour, the full bowl sank and pulled hidden cords! A bird whistled, a dragon dropped a ball, and cymbals clashed—blending ideas from India, China, Greece, and Islam.

parent_discussion.question: Which three everyday modern English words come directly from Muhammad al-Khwarizmi's name, his book 'al-Jabr', and Arabic 'sifr'?

parent_discussion.answer: Treatment was completely free, and recovering poor patients were given clean clothes and pocket money to rest safely at home.

guided_reading.extract: During Caliph Harun al-Rashid's reign, a tired porter named Hindbad set his heavy load outside a cool Baghdad house. Smelling sweet rosewater inside, he sighed at his hard life. Kindly, rich Sinbad the Sailor called him indoors, piled his plate with spiced food, and told his sea tale. "Friend, I never won these silks while resting on soft cushions! As a young man, I walked into Baghdad's shaded bazaars. There I spent my last silver dirhams on bales of cloth, cut glass, and sweet dates. With brave traders, I sailed down the fast River Tigris to the port of Basra." guided_reading.extract:
As hot Iraqi afternoons cooled beneath tall badgir windcatcher towers, Baghdad families sat beside courtyard fountains sipping sweet lemon and rosewater drinks. Between plates of spiced almonds, two players spread a sixty-four-square leather mat and set out smooth turquoise and brown shatranj pieces. Poets loved chanting riddles about this bloodless game of wits:
Two silent armies face each other on a square-cut plain,
Where neither drum beats loud nor drop of blood is ever spilled!
Swift horses leap across the lines while war-elephants advance,
And loyal viziers guard their Shah behind a footmen's wall.
No human faces mark their clay, just curves of turquoise glaze,
Yet sharper than a steel-tipped spear is every silent move!
One careless step—a trap springs shut around the cornered king,
And laughter rings across the tiles at "Shah mat!" in the shade!
Centuries later, travellers carried shatranj into Spain and Britain, turning Shah mat into checkmate!

guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive

guided_reading.author_context: When Mongol boulders smashed Baghdad's brick walls in February 1258, flames ruined the House of Wisdom. Read aloud to discover how brave scholars and distant libraries saved Golden Age science for our world today!

vocabVault.def: The Mongol commander whose vast army surrounded and captured Abbasid Baghdad in January–February AD 1258.

guided_reading.extract: In January 1258, the ground by the River Tigris shook under thousands of Mongol horses. Hulagu Khan's men built tall wooden trebuchets to fling big rocks at Baghdad's brick walls. When the city fell in February, dark smoke rose over broken palaces and the House of Wisdom. Yet five hundred years of bright science did not burn away! Brave star-watcher al-Tusi begged to save boxes of rare scrolls. He packed 400,000 books onto strong mules bound for his new star tower in the north! Better still, cheap rag paper meant spare copies sat safe in Cairo, Damascus, and Al-Andalus in Spain. Far west in Spanish Toledo, Muslim, Jewish, and Christian thinkers worked side by side. By warm candlelight, they turned al-Khwarizmi's 0–9 sums and Ibn al-Haytham's light tests into Latin! Every time you write zero or snap a photo today, Baghdad's bright torch shines on.
